To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
pH responsive calixarene-based hydrogels can be obtained in water at low concentrations.
water soluble amphiphilc calix[8]-arenes form pH-responsive supramolecular hydrogel at sub-millimal concentration.

water-soluble amphiphilic derivatives of calix[8]-arenes form pH-responsive hydrogels at low concentrations, that the hydrogel formation is driven by the self-assembling of the calix[8](OH)4 molecules into supramolecular fibers, and that the fibers can be used to build up 3D hydrogel networks by crosslinking the fibers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the synthesis and characterization of new calix[8]-based amphiphiles and the study of their self-assembly processes at nanometric scale.
the synthesis of new water-soluble amphiphilic derivatives of calix[8]-arenes and the study of their self-assembly properties.
the development of supramolecular hydrogelators and their use as building blocks to fabricate functional materials.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
calixarene hydrogels can be used as a model to understand and control self-assembly processes at the nanometric level.
the hydrogelation of the calixarene derivatives is a complex and multistep process.

the supramolecular hydrogelation of amphiphilic water-soluble calix[8]-arenes is governed by a combination of intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonding, hydrophobic, and van der Waals forces) and the electrostatic interactions between the calixarene and the surface.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
calix[8](O-CH2-OCH2)4(OH)4(OH2)4, a pH responsive hydrogelator, can be used to build a pH sensitive hydrogel.

we have shown that the supramolecular hydrogelators are able to self-organize into nanostructures, and the nanostructures are able to organize into macroscopic hydrogels, and that the nanostructures and the hydrogels are able to self-heal.
calixarenes are a class of macrocyclic molecules with a great potential in supramolecular chemistry and in the field of nanotechnology.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the self-assembling processes are driven by the electrostatic interactions between the charged calixarene hydrogels and the surface.
the supramolecular assembly of these amphiphilic molecules is strongly dependent on the pH and the charge of the surface.
hydrogelation occurs by a mechanism that involves the formation of nanometric fibers that self-assemble in the bulk to form the macroscopic network.
